title: Competing Against Luck: The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice
author: Clayton M. Christensen
Taddy Hall
Karen Dillon
David S. Duncan
target_audience: Anyone interested in how successful innovation works
core_themes: Innovation driven by ‘Jobs to Be Done’
Moving from chance to deliberate innovation
primary_purpose: To present and explain the ‘Jobs to Be Done’ theory, offering a framework for businesses to better understand why customers make the choices they do, and showing how innovation can be made more predictable and successful by focusing on the progress customers are trying to achieve.

structure_format.organization: Divided into thematic chapters, starting with foundational concepts, then progressing through case studies, application, and practical guidelines

key_concepts_lessons: 'Jobs to Be Done' theory — customers 'hire' products and services to get specific jobs accomplished in their lives.
Understanding the context around customer needs is essential to creating and marketing effective products.
Innovation success is less about luck and more about deeply understanding what causes customers to make choices.
Companies often fail by focusing on product features rather than the progress customers truly seek.
Successful innovation requires defining the 'job', shaping the solution around it, and aligning organizational processes accordingly.
By focusing on the job, companies can predictably create solutions that customers want—reducing randomness in new product success.
notable_features: Popularized ‘Jobs Theory’ in mainstream business practice
Uses well-known industry examples (e.g., McDonald's milkshakes, Airbnb, Intuit)
Bridges academic research and real-world application
Offers practical checklists and diagnostic questions for businesses
cultural_historical_context: Published at a time of rapid technological disruption, when traditional innovation processes were yielding inconsistent results, the book builds on Christensen’s earlier work on disruptive innovation and addresses persistent challenges in launching successful products in a crowded market.
reception_impact: Received positive reviews for making the ‘Jobs to Be Done’ framework accessible
Influential in strategy, product development, and innovation circles
Adopted by organizations as a foundation for customer-centric innovation
Praised for clear explanations and actionable business insights, though some critics found it repetitive or conceptually dense
comparable_titles: The Innovator’s Dilemma by Clayton M. Christensen
Blue Ocean Strategy by W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne
What Customers Want by Anthony Ulwick
